summary: In 1845 the United States annexed Texas, which had broken away from Mexico in 1836. Mexico had never recognised Texan independence and had threatened war over annexation, and the two countries also disputed the border: Texas claimed the Rio Grande, Mexico the Nueces River farther north. President James K. Polk, who also wanted California and New Mexico, sent John Slidell to buy them and moved Zachary Taylor's army to the Rio Grande. A Mexican attack on a US patrol in the disputed zone on 25 April 1846 led Congress to declare war. Taylor won at Palo Alto, Resaca de la Palma and Monterrey and held off Santa Anna at Buena Vista, while US forces occupied New Mexico and, after a Californio uprising, California. In March 1847 Winfield Scott landed at Veracruz and fought his way inland, taking Mexico City in September. The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo of 1848 gave the United States about 55 percent of Mexico's territory for $15 million, and the fight over slavery in the new lands sharpened the sectional crisis in the United States.
casualties: An estimated 13,000 Americans died, about 1,700 of them killed in battle and most of the rest from disease, while Mexican military and civilian deaths are estimated at up to about 25,000.

brief.hook: After the United States annexed Texas, a quarrel over its border and President Polk's wish for California and New Mexico brought war with Mexico.

sides.who: The United States regular army, state volunteers and navy, with American settlers of the Bear Flag revolt in California
The Mexican Republic's army and national guard, though only 7 of its 19 states sent men, arms or money

brief.resultLine: Scott's army took Mexico City in September 1847, and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848, handed Mexico's northern lands to the United States.

strategies.name: Flying artillery
strategies.text: At Palo Alto in May 1846, American gunners fired their light cannon, galloped to a new spot and fired again. They outgunned the Mexican artillery and broke up cavalry charges.

strategies.name: Scott's landing at Veracruz
strategies.text: Striking at the heart of Mexico, Scott landed his army on the beach near Veracruz in March 1847 without losing a man, took the port after twenty days and marched inland on the capital.

strategies.name: A nation divided
strategies.text: Mexico changed presidents four times in 1846, liberals and conservatives fought each other, and conservatives revolted in early 1847 against seizing Church property to pay for the war.

impact: Mexico lost about 55 percent of its territory, some 525,000 square miles, for $15 million.
The United States now reached the Pacific, taking in California, Nevada, Utah and parts of several future states.
The fight over slavery in the new lands, begun with the Wilmot Proviso, deepened the split that led to civil war.

details: Texas had become the 28th US state on 29 December 1845, and Mexico, which still regarded it as Mexican, had broken off diplomatic relations. Polk's envoy John Slidell, sent with an offer to buy the Rio Grande border, California and New Mexico, was refused. Polk then ordered General Zachary Taylor, camped on the Nueces since 1845, into the disputed land beyond it. In March 1846 Taylor's army reached the Rio Grande opposite Matamoros and began building a fort, later called Fort Texas.

On 23 April 1846 Mexico's president, General Mariano Paredes, declared a defensive war. Two days later a large Mexican cavalry force that had crossed the Rio Grande surrounded a patrol of about 70 US dragoons under Captain Seth Thornton at a ranch upriver from Taylor's fort, killing 11 and capturing 52. Taylor reported to Washington that hostilities had begun, and Polk, who had already been preparing to ask Congress for war, used the clash to argue that Mexico had started it.

General Mariano Arista crossed the Rio Grande with most of his army, threatening Taylor's supply base at Point Isabel on the coast, and Taylor marched off to secure it. From 3 May 1846 Mexican artillery in Matamoros shelled the fort he had left behind, keeping up the bombardment for some 160 hours. Its commander, Major Jacob Brown, was one of two defenders killed, and the post was renamed Fort Brown in his honour, giving its name to the later city of Brownsville.

Returning to relieve the fort, Taylor's roughly 2,300 men met Arista's army of about 3,700 on the coastal prairie of Palo Alto on 8 May 1846. The battle was fought largely with artillery. Mobile US 'flying artillery' batteries fired, moved and fired again, causing heavy losses that the Mexican guns could not match. Mexican casualties were about 102 killed and 129 wounded against nine Americans killed; Major Samuel Ringgold was mortally wounded. That evening Arista pulled back to the south.

Arista made a new stand the next day in a dry riverbed, or resaca, lined with thick brush on the road to Matamoros. In close fighting on 9 May 1846 US dragoons captured Mexican artillery, and the Mexican army broke and fled back across the Rio Grande. Fort Texas was relieved. Later in May Taylor crossed the river and occupied Matamoros, which Arista had abandoned, and the war moved south into northern Mexico.

Polk asked Congress for war, arguing that Mexico had begun hostilities on American soil, and Congress approved the declaration on 13 May 1846. Critics, mostly Whigs, accused Polk of provoking the war by sending troops into disputed land; among them, later in the war, was the young congressman Abraham Lincoln, whose 'spot resolutions' challenged Polk to name the spot where the first blood had been shed. Mexico's Congress formally declared war on 7 July 1846.

In Mexico's thinly held province of Alta California, American settlers in the Sacramento Valley, emboldened by the US Army explorer John C. Frémont and his armed party, rose against the Mexican authorities. On 14 June 1846 they seized the barracks at Sonoma and raised a flag bearing a grizzly bear and a star, proclaiming the California Republic under William B. Ide. It lasted 25 days: on 9 July the US flag was raised at Sonoma, and the rebels joined Frémont's California Battalion.

Commodore John D. Sloat's Pacific Squadron landed sailors and marines at Monterey, the capital of Alta California, on 7 July 1846 and took the town without a shot. Two days later another landing party took Yerba Buena, the future San Francisco. Commodore Robert Stockton, who succeeded Sloat, joined forces with Frémont, and on 13 August 1846 US troops entered Los Angeles unopposed. Within weeks of the first landings, California seemed to be won.

The defeats on the Rio Grande discredited the centralist government of Paredes, who was overthrown in the summer of 1846. Federalist liberals restored the Constitution of 1824, and José Mariano Salas became acting president. Santa Anna, in exile in Cuba, returned in August after the US Navy let him through its blockade of the Gulf coast, in the belief that he would make peace. Instead he took command of the army and raised a new force at San Luis Potosí.

General Stephen W. Kearny led the Army of the West, about 1,600 regulars and volunteers, from Fort Leavenworth down the Santa Fe Trail. Governor Manuel Armijo gathered militia at Apache Canyon east of Santa Fe, then withdrew without fighting and fled south to Chihuahua. Kearny entered Santa Fe and on 18 August 1846 took possession of New Mexico, declaring himself military governor and setting up a civil government. Leaving a garrison behind, he set out for California the following month.

Taylor advanced on Monterrey, a fortified city in Nuevo León held by General Pedro de Ampudia. From 20 September 1846 his troops attacked the forts on the city's outskirts and then fought their way street by street into the centre, taking heavy losses. On 24 September Ampudia agreed to give up Monterrey in return for an eight-week armistice and the free withdrawal of his army. Polk disliked the terms, and Taylor later ended the truce by occupying Saltillo.

The small US garrison left in Los Angeles under Archibald Gillespie imposed strict rules that angered the Californios, the Mexican residents of the province. In late September 1846 they rose under José María Flores and forced the garrison to withdraw, and the revolt spread across southern California, where Mexican control was restored for the rest of the year. US forces could not retake the city that autumn, and the conquest of California had to be fought again.

Kearny reached southern California after a hard march across the desert with a small force of dragoons. On 6 December 1846, near the village of San Pasqual, about 150 Americans attacked some 100 Californio lancers under Andrés Pico. The lancers, expert horsemen, turned on the scattered American column and cut it up in about half an hour; 22 Americans were killed and Kearny himself was wounded. Pinned on a hilltop, his force was rescued by sailors and marines sent from San Diego.

Stockton and Kearny marched north from San Diego with a combined force of sailors, marines and soldiers. They defeated Flores's Californios at the Río San Gabriel on 8 January 1847 and at La Mesa the next day, and entered Los Angeles unopposed on 10 January. On 13 January Andrés Pico and John C. Frémont signed the Articles of Capitulation at Cahuenga Pass, which allowed the Californios to go home and ended the fighting in California.

Many New Mexicans resented the American occupation. On 19 January 1847 Hispano and Pueblo insurgents at Taos killed the new governor, Charles Bent, and other officials, and the next day attacked Turley's mill at Arroyo Hondo. Colonel Sterling Price marched north from Santa Fe with more than 300 soldiers and volunteers and besieged the rebels in Taos Pueblo in early February. About 150 rebels were killed and some 400 captured, against seven Americans dead, and the revolt was crushed.

Many of Taylor's regulars had been sent to join Winfield Scott's planned landing at Veracruz. Santa Anna marched north from San Luis Potosí, losing thousands of men on the way, and on 22–23 February 1847 attacked Taylor's roughly 4,600 men, mostly volunteers, at the pass of La Angostura near the Buena Vista hacienda south of Saltillo. His army of about 15,000 came close to breaking the US line. Both sides claimed victory, but Santa Anna withdrew, and the battle made Taylor a national hero.

Polk decided to strike at Mexico City from the sea. On 9 March 1847 Winfield Scott put his army ashore on the beaches south of Veracruz without opposition, the first major amphibious landing in US history. His troops surrounded the walled port, and from 22 March siege and naval guns bombarded it, killing hundreds of civilians. The defenders asked for terms on 26 March, and on 29 March the city and the island fortress of San Juan de Ulúa surrendered, with some 3,000 soldiers taken prisoner.

Scott marched inland along the National Road, eager to leave the coast before the yellow-fever season. Santa Anna blocked the road at the mountain pass of Cerro Gordo with a large army in strong positions. Scouts, among them Captain Robert E. Lee, found a path around the Mexican left, and on 18 April 1847 Scott's army of about 8,500 attacked from flank and front. The Mexican army collapsed, losing more than 1,000 killed and wounded and about 3,000 prisoners, against some 400 US casualties.

After waiting months at Puebla for reinforcements, Scott advanced on Mexico City in August 1847. On 19–20 August his army routed a Mexican force at Contreras (Padierna) and then stormed the fortified convent of Churubusco, defended to the last by Mexican troops and the Saint Patrick's Battalion, made up mostly of Irish and other immigrant deserters from the US Army. US losses at Churubusco were more than 1,000 killed, wounded and missing. An armistice followed, but peace talks broke down on 6 September.

When the armistice ended, Scott sent William Worth's division against Molino del Rey, a group of stone mill buildings about a thousand yards west of the hill of Chapultepec, where he believed cannon were being cast. Mexican troops put up a fierce defence on 8 September 1847, and the Americans took the buildings only at heavy cost to both sides. Scott then turned on Chapultepec Castle, the hilltop fortress and military college that guarded the western approaches to the capital.

After a bombardment that began on 12 September, US troops stormed Chapultepec Castle on the morning of 13 September 1847 and took it by about 9 a.m. Among its roughly 830 defenders were cadets of the military college; six who died there are honoured in Mexico as the Niños Héroes. Nearby, thirty captured members of the Saint Patrick's Battalion were hanged at the moment the US flag replaced the Mexican one over the castle. US troops then fought their way to the city gates of Belén and San Cosme.

Santa Anna withdrew his remaining troops from the capital during the night, and on 14 September 1847 Scott's army marched into Mexico City and raised the US flag over the National Palace. Scott became military governor of the occupied city. Santa Anna soon gave up the presidency, and a new Mexican government gathered at Querétaro, while guerrillas attacked US supply lines between the capital and the coast. Fighting dwindled, but peace still had to be negotiated.

Santa Anna made a final attempt to cut Scott's communications by besieging the US garrison left at Puebla. A relief column under General Joseph Lane, marching inland from Veracruz, defeated his troops at Huamantla on 9 October 1847, after which Lane's men sacked the town. Puebla was relieved on 12 October. It was the last battle Santa Anna fought in the war, and the remaining Mexican resistance was left to guerrilla bands.

The US envoy Nicholas Trist, ignoring Polk's order recalling him, negotiated with Mexico's government, and on 2 February 1848 a treaty was signed at Guadalupe Hidalgo, just north of Mexico City. Mexico gave up all claims to Texas, with the border on the Rio Grande, and ceded about 55 percent of its territory: present-day California, Nevada, Utah, New Mexico, most of Arizona and parts of several other states. The United States paid $15 million and assumed up to $3.25 million in its citizens' claims against Mexico.

Polk, angry with Trist but content with the terms, sent the treaty to the Senate, where some members wanted to annex more of Mexico and others wanted no territory at all. The Senate approved it on 10 March 1848 by 38 votes to 14, after deleting Article X, which protected Mexican land grants. Formal hostilities had ended on 6 March. The war left a bitter question behind: the Wilmot Proviso, which would have barred slavery from the new lands, had passed the House in 1847 but failed in the Senate.

Mexico's Congress, meeting at Querétaro, debated the amended treaty and approved it in May 1848. Ratifications were exchanged there on 30 May, and the treaty was proclaimed in the United States on 4 July. US troops left Mexico City in June and had evacuated Mexico by August. Mexicans living in the ceded lands could stay and keep their property; those who did not choose Mexican citizenship within a year would become citizens of the United States.
